the enteric microbiome is involved in bidirectional signaling between the gut and the brain, and this signaling may be important in the regulation of gastrointestinal function, as well as in the pathophysiological mechanisms of gastrointestinal disorders, such as functional gastrointestinal disorders and inflammatory bowel disease.
the enteric microbiome is a key component of the brain– gut–enteric microbiome axis and that disruption of this axis is involved in the pathogenesis of functional and inflammatory bowel diseases.
the gut microbiota can affect brain function and behavior via the gut–brain axis, and that the gut microbiome is a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of psychiatric disorders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms and clinical implications of brain–gut and brain–gut enteric microbiota axis interactions.
the role of the enterogastric microbiota in the pathophysiological mechanisms of acute and chronic intestinal diseases, including functional and IBD.
the role of the enterocromaffin cells in the regulation of the gut microbiota.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain–gust–enteric microbiome axis is a very important mechanism for regulation of gut function, and disruption of this axis can result in gastrointestinal disease.
the gut microbiota has a role in brain–gut communication, and that the brain–gib–gut axis is a complex, bidirectional communication system between the enteric flora and the nervous system.

the enteric flora has the potential to modulate brain function and that the enteric microbiome is an important factor to be considered in the pathogenesis of functional gastrointestinal disorders and inflammatory bowel diseases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated the importance of the enteric microbiome in the pathogenesis of functional bowel disorders.
the gut microbiome is a key factor in the development of a healthy brain and a healthy gut.
the brain and the gut are not separate, isolated entities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the enteric flora has a major role in modulating gastrointestinal function, and that disruption of the bidirectional brain–enteric microbiotic axis may be involved in gastrointestinal disease states.
the enteric microbiome is not just a collection of commensal bacteria that reside in the gut but a complex and important organ that communicates with the brain and other parts of the body.
the enteric flora is a key player in the bidirectional communication between the brain and the gut.
